feedback: If arrows appear only near the poles: ask the learner to test positions directly out to the side and below/above the magnet. The needle lines up with the magnet's field there too, which shows the field surrounds the magnet in all directions, getting weaker with distance.

If field lines are drawn crossing or without arrows: remind that each point has one needle direction, so lines cannot cross and must carry an arrow (pointing the way the needle's north-seeking end points, from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole).
If the learner says 'there's no field between my lines': have them drop the compass into a gap — it still deflects, so the field is continuous and the lines are just a representation.
If densest lines are drawn at the centre of the bar: compare with the iron-filings pattern, which clumps at the POLES — closer lines mean stronger field.
activities.intendedInsight: The field is a continuous region of force filling the space all around the magnet, not something that exists only at the poles or only where a line is drawn; the compass and filings merely PROBE it. Direction and strength are two readings of one invisible field.
learnerActions: Place a plotting compass far from any magnet and note that it settles pointing north.

Position a bar magnet, then move the compass step-by-step to many positions around it; at each position draw a small arrow pointing the way the needle's NORTH-SEEKING end points — this is the field direction, running outward from the magnet's north pole toward its south pole.
Join the arrows to trace continuous field lines, working outward from one pole and around to the other.

Deliberately place the compass out to the SIDE of the magnet (not just near the poles) and record which way the needle points compared with when the magnet was absent. Near the magnet the needle lines up with the magnet's field, but with some magnet orientations that direction can match its original northward direction, so also try turning the magnet.
Overlay or compare an iron-filings pattern on the same magnet, noting that filings show shape/strength while the compass shows direction — two readings of one field.
Bring a second magnet nearby and re-map a few points to see how the whole pattern changes (like poles push lines apart, opposite poles link them).
activities.title: Map the field with a plotting compass

feedback: If the learner says the needle is pulled toward the North Star, 'the cold', or 'north as a place': introduce Earth as a giant magnet with a field the needle aligns to, and deflect the needle with a bar magnet to prove the needle is itself magnetic.

Full understanding connects needle-as-magnet with Earth's field; a partial response states separate facts (Earth has a field; poles attract/repel) without explaining why the same end always points north.
The geographic-north/magnetic-south detail is enrichment; do not treat confusion about it as a core error at this stage.
activities.intendedInsight: A compass works because the needle is itself a small magnet that aligns with Earth's magnetic field (when away from other magnets and iron), which is why the same end consistently points (magnetic) north and the compass can be used for navigation.
learnerActions: Draw the Earth as a bar magnet with a compass needle aligning to its field.
Explain why a compass needle's SAME end always turns to point north, in terms of the needle being a tiny magnet aligning with Earth's field.
Reason about transfer: if you took the compass to Australia, would the same end still point north? Why?

Discuss the enrichment point: the Earth's magnetic pole near geographic north behaves like a magnetic south-type pole, so the needle's north pole is attracted to it (opposites attract) — flagged as enrichment, not required.
activities.title: Earth as a magnet and the compass for navigation

feedback: If a learner believes the field is only the flat pattern they drew on the table: have them hold the compass a short distance above the magnet and watch it still respond to the magnet, showing the field extends in all directions.
Keep this scoped to the 3D-nature point; the examined drawing, direction and navigation skills are fully served in 2D.
activities.intendedInsight: The magnetic field is genuinely three-dimensional — it surrounds the magnet in every direction — and the familiar 2D field-line diagram is one plane through that volume.
learnerActions: Move a compass or sensor through the space around a magnet at different heights and positions — above, below and to the sides — not just in the flat tabletop plane.

Record how the needle responds at each height and position close to the magnet (the effect weakens with distance), concluding the field occupies a VOLUME around the magnet, not only the flat textbook pattern.
Relate the 3D volume back to the 2D field-line diagram, recognising the diagram as one slice through the full field.
activities.title: The field in three dimensions (narrow complement)
